lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Supervised application: handling conflict or a mistake professionally

objective: Learners rehearse reporting a workplace mistake to a supervisor using a structured script, with a trusted adult playing the supervisor role, so owning a mistake professionally feels routine rather than terrifying when it happens for real.
scenario: Given a short fictional workplace-mistake scenario (for example, sending something to the wrong recipient, or being late without notice), the learner rehearses reporting it out loud to a trusted adult playing the supervisor, using a three-part structure (what happened, what I'm doing about it, what I need), then revises based on feedback.
safetyNotes: No audio or video recording is made; the adult gives live feedback and the learner writes notes afterward.
The mistake scenario is fictional and does not require the learner to disclose or discuss any real mistake from their own life.

simulationAlternative.description: If no adult is available to role-play the supervisor, the learner writes both sides of the conversation as a short script, then reads only their own side aloud once and self-checks it against the same look-fors.

tasks.directions: Before practicing, write down what makes reporting your own mistake feel harder than reporting someone else's.

prompts.text: What is one reason reporting your own mistake might feel harder than pointing out someone else's?

tasks.directions: With your adult playing the supervisor, report the fictional mistake using the three-part structure.

prompts.text: I stated clearly what happened, without minimizing or over-explaining.
I stated what I was already doing about it.
I stated what I needed, if anything, from the supervisor.

tasks.directions: Revise your report based on the feedback and write the improved version.

prompts.text: Write your revised version of the mistake report, and explain what you changed based on the feedback.
In the fictional scenario, would it have been better to report the mistake sooner, and how would you recognize that same moment in a real situation?

remediation: If the learner's report spends most of its time minimizing or making excuses rather than stating what happened and what's being done, reteach the three-part structure explicitly, modeling one complete example, before the learner retries their own report using that structure.
extension: Have the learner practice a second, harder version: reporting a mistake that was only discovered by someone else first, not self-caught, using the same three-part structure adapted for that harder situation.
